sections.html:
The Clackamas County seat, Oregon City stands along the Willamette near the southern limit of metro Portland. It rests on two levels: a bench by the river and an upper section on a basalt bluff, joined since 1915 by a historic elevator. The Willamette separates it from West Linn, and the Clackamas River separates it from Gladstone.

Estimated population on July 1, 2025 was 38,175, compared with 37,572 in 2020. If your house is on the bluff, say so in the listing, because buyers weigh slope, views and walking access.

The $555,800 median is a citywide midpoint. It does not tell you what a particular house will bring, so compare against recent sales on your own street.

The city recognizes 12 neighborhood associations. Three come up most often.

  • McLoughlin sits on the bluff above downtown, with many older homes plus the library, a pool and a hospital.
  • Canemah is a narrow strip along OR 99E between the river and a bluff. It began in 1845 as its own city and was annexed later.
  • Two Rivers is the low, mostly commercial part of town, home to downtown and Clackamette Park.

Most of the 44.81 inches of annual rain falls between November and March. Months of wet weather are hard on roofs, decks and retaining walls, and a bluff lot adds drainage to what an inspector will check. If you have a wall or a slope, be ready to show that it has held up.

In a designated historic area, exterior changes need city review before the work begins. The Canemah National Register District and the McLoughlin Conservation District, which spans 1st through 12th streets, are the main ones.

  • Windows, doors, siding changes and additions on designated structures get special review.
  • Type I review is a staff decision for limited alterations that fit clear policies.
  • Type III review goes to the Historic Review Board for discretionary calls, additions under 30% of the original structure, and new construction or larger additions.

Planning staff can say whether your address is designated: ocplanning@orcity.org or 503-722-3789. Anyone planning a remodel will ask, so learn the answer before you list.

The Department of Assessment and Taxation bills Oregon City property from its office at 150 Beavercreek Road, Suite 135. The phone number is 503-655-8671.

The three installments fall on November 15, February 15 and May 15; the printed bill shows the exact dates for the year. Full payment by the first date earns a 3% discount, and two-thirds earns 2%. Value appeals go to the Property Value Appeals Board by December 31.

At closing the title company pays the current installment and divides the tax year between buyer and seller.

A signed disclosure statement goes to each buyer who writes an offer on a one-to-four-unit home, as a general rule, and that buyer can revoke within five business days of delivery unless the right was waived. ORS 105.470 leaves out court-appointed sellers, such as personal representatives and trustees, and financial institutions that took the property in foreclosure.

sections.h2: Listing, selling alone or an as-is cash sale
sections.html: Three routes are open to a homeowner in town: hire an agent, handle the sale yourself, or take an as-is cash offer. Cash buyers each write their own terms, so set timelines, repair duties and closing costs side by side on paper.

Without a mortgage lender, there is no loan approval to wait on. The order of events:

  1. Describe the property, its shape and your target date.
  2. Get the offer in writing and see who pays closing costs and who owes repairs.
  3. Escrow opens at a title company that hunts for liens and tax debt.
  4. Both sides sign, the deed is recorded and your proceeds are released.

Owing back taxes will not stop a sale. The balance and its interest are deducted from your proceeds when you close. Request a payoff number up front so you can see your net before agreeing on a price, and call 503-655-8671 to learn what the county shows unpaid.

• A photo ID with the deed's exact name.
  • The most recent tax bill.
  • Mortgage lender and loan number, if there is a payoff.
  • Lease and deposit records for a tenant.
  • For a house in a historic area, any city approvals for past exterior work.
  • Keys, openers and warranty or permit papers.

A title or escrow office handles the signing. After the deed is recorded, your mortgage payoff and any taxes owed come out, the tax year is split, and you receive what remains. In a cash sale, no lender sets a deadline, so the date can follow your move.

sections.h2: Pricing and timing on the bluff versus the flats
sections.html:
Your house's spot in the city changes both the listing language and the buyer reaction. A bluff house in McLoughlin is judged on older-home charm, views and walkability, and buyers will look at the foundation, the retaining walls and how water runs off the lot. A house on the lower bench is judged more on access and noise. Whichever you own, a buyer's agent will bring comparable sales from the same part of town, so expect your price to be tested against those.

If the house stands inside a historic area, mention that early. Some buyers love it and others want to know about review rules before they make an offer.

sections.h2: If a tenant lives in the house
sections.html: Find the lease, then write down its end date and any deposit held. Let the tenant know when you intend to list and settle showing times in writing. Buyers who hear about a tenant at the start can plan for one; a surprise during escrow can sink the deal. Decide whether the buyer will take the house occupied or whether you will deliver it empty, and set the closing date to match.

sections.h2: Questions to ask the title company
sections.html:
• What liens or unpaid taxes show up against the property?
  • What is my payoff figure today?
  • Which closing costs fall to me, and which to the buyer?
  • How will the current tax year be split?
  • What do you need from me to close on the date we picked?

The answers give you a realistic net number before you commit to any offer.

Walk the property as a stranger would. Look at the roof line, the gutters, any deck and each retaining wall, because wet winters reveal weakness there first. Fix drips and loose boards, and have documents about past work in a single folder. If a buyer asks about the elevator, the bluff or the historic rules, a confident answer shows you know the house.

faqs.q: What county is Oregon City in?
faqs.a: Clackamas County. Oregon City is the county seat, and the county's assessment and taxation office is in the city.

faqs.q: How many people live in Oregon City?
faqs.a: The July 1, 2025 estimate is 38,175. The 2020 count was 37,572.

faqs.q: Why is Oregon City important in Oregon history?
faqs.a: It was the end of the Oregon Trail, the first U.S. city west of the Rockies to incorporate, in 1844, and capital of Oregon Territory from 1848 to 1851.

faqs.q: Do Oregon City historic district rules affect selling?
faqs.a: They can. Exterior changes to designated structures need staff or Historic Review Board review, so a buyer who wants to alter a Canemah or McLoughlin house will ask about it.

faqs.q: When are property taxes due in Clackamas County?
faqs.a: November 15, February 15 and May 15. Full payment by the first date earns a 3% discount, and two-thirds earns 2%.
